content: A fundamental unit is a basic unit of measurement for physical quantities, from which all other units can be derived. In the context of measurement, physical quantities are measurable properties of the world, such as time, distance, velocity, mass, momentum, energy, and weight. Units are used to describe the magnitude of these quantities. For example, the dimensions of a package to be mailed might be described as 12 inches by 8 inches by 4 inches. The term dimension typically refers to the category of physical quantity being measured, such as length, time, mass, momentum, or energy, as explored in dimensional analysis. A system of fundamental quantities, or fundamental dimensions, is structured so that all other physical quantities or dimensions can be derived from them. Traditionally, the fundamental dimensions of physical quantities include mass, length, time, and temperature. However, in principle, other fundamental quantities could be chosen. Some physicists argue that temperature is not a truly fundamental dimension because it represents energy per particle per degree of freedom, which can be expressed in terms of energy (or mass, length, and time). Additionally, some physicists recognize electric charge as a separate fundamental dimension, even though it can be expressed in terms of mass, length, and time in certain unit systems, such as the electrostatic CGS system. There are also physicists who question the very existence of incompatible fundamental quantities. In the International System of Units (SI), the fundamental units are the kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, and mole. The metre and candela were previously considered fundamental units but have since been redefined in terms of other units. However, they are still regarded as SI base units for historical reasons. Other units, such as the newton, joule, and volt, are derived from the SI base units and are therefore classified as SI derived units. For instance, the dimension of speed is defined as length divided by time, so its unit, metres per second (m/s), can be derived from the fundamental unit of seconds (with the metre also being defined in terms of the second). An important concept in dimensional analysis is that fundamental units can be viewed as the basis of a specialized vector space, known as the space of all units. This vector space is defined over the field of rational numbers, where vector addition corresponds to the multiplication of units, and scalar multiplication corresponds to the exponentiation of units. Not all physically significant values have associated units. Dimensionless numbers are frequently encountered in various scientific fields. In fact, dimensionless quantities are fundamentally what we measure, even when dealing with quantities that have dimensions. When measuring a physical quantity, it is always compared against a standard of the same dimension. For example, when measuring length with a ruler or tape measure, one is essentially counting the tick marks on the ruler, which serves as a standard for length measurement. The result is a dimensionless number. However, when this number is expressed alongside a dimensional unit (e.g., metres or inches), it conceptually becomes a dimensional quantity.
